client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Everything just feels kind of gray and flat — like I go through the motions of my day but nothing feels meaningful or enjoyable anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd at least try.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up and try, even when part of you doubts it will help — and I want you to know that quiet, heavy feeling you're describing, where the color seems drained out of everyday life, makes complete sense after losing someone you loved. Grief can make the world feel muted and distant, and that's not a sign something is permanently wrong with you. I'm curious — when you think about your grandmother, is there a particular moment or memory that feels most present for you right now?

client: There's this one Sunday morning that keeps coming back to me — she used to make these thick, sweet pancakes, and we'd sit at her kitchen table for hours just talking about nothing in particular. I can almost smell the kitchen when I think about it, and then I feel this sharp pang because I know that's just gone now, that table, that kitchen, her. It's like the memory is beautiful and painful at the exact same time, and I don't really know what to do with that.
therapist: That memory is so vivid and tender — the smell of the kitchen, the unhurried Sunday mornings — and it makes sense that something so beautiful would carry an ache right alongside it, because the depth of the pain is really just a reflection of how meaningful she was to you. In CBT we sometimes notice how our minds can get stuck in an "all or nothing" place, where we feel like the loss has erased the good — but I wonder if there's another way to hold it, where that memory isn't just a reminder of what's gone, but also evidence of something real and lasting that she gave you. What do you think she would say if she knew that Sunday morning still lives so vividly in you?

client: I think she'd probably smile and say something like "of course it does, that's what I intended" — she was that kind of person, very deliberate about creating those moments. But I guess I'm a little skeptical of the idea that reframing it as "lasting" makes the pain any easier, because right now it mostly just feels like a door that's been locked shut forever. I want to believe there's something still there that isn't just loss, but I'm not sure I actually feel that yet.
therapist: That response about her — "of course it does, that's what I intended" — tells me so much about who she was, and honestly, the fact that you can still hear her voice so clearly is quietly remarkable. And I really appreciate your honesty in pushing back, because you're right that reframing isn't a magic switch, and I don't want to rush you past the very real pain of that locked door — you don't have to feel the "lasting" part yet, you just have to notice that you're not quite ready to let go of it either, which is different from it being gone. What do you think it would feel like, even just a little, if that door weren't locked forever but just... closed for now?

client: I think "closed for now" actually feels a little less suffocating than "locked forever" — like there's at least some air in that idea. But then I immediately feel guilty for even entertaining it, like I'm somehow betraying her or minimizing how much I've lost by trying to make myself feel better. I don't know if that makes sense, but the guilt kind of sneaks in every time I get close to feeling even slightly okay about any of it.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and it's actually one of the most common and tender traps grief can set for us — this belief that staying in pain is somehow proof of love, and that finding even a breath of relief is a kind of betrayal. But I'd gently invite you to hold that up against what you just told us about her: she was *deliberate* about creating joy for you, she intended those Sunday mornings to stay with you — does it really sound like her intention was for you to feel guilty every time you found a moment of peace? What do you think she would say about that guilt if she could?

client: She would absolutely tell me to stop being ridiculous and go enjoy something — she had no patience for unnecessary suffering, she used to say that pretty directly actually. But knowing what she would say and actually feeling permission to act on it are two completely different things, and I think that gap is where I keep getting stuck. It's like I understand it intellectually but my chest still tightens every time I try to let myself off the hook.
therapist: She sounds like she was wonderfully no-nonsense, and there's something almost tender about the fact that you can hear her so clearly telling you to stop — her voice is still with you, still looking out for you. That gap you're naming, between knowing something in your head and feeling it settle in your body, is real and important, and it's actually exactly where a lot of our work can happen — because that chest tightening is your nervous system still trying to protect you, not evidence that the guilt is true or deserved. I'm wondering, when that tightness shows up, what's the specific thought that seems to come with it — is there a particular thing you're afraid will happen if you actually let yourself off the hook?

client: I think the fear is that if I stop hurting, I'll start forgetting — like the grief is the last thread connecting me to her, and if I let it ease up, she'll somehow become less real or less present to me. It sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but there's this deep worry that moving forward means leaving her behind. And I can't quite shake the feeling that she deserves better than to just become a memory I visit less and less.
therapist: What you just said doesn't sound irrational at all — it sounds like love trying to find a way to hold on, and it's one of the most human fears there is. But I want to gently offer something: that vivid Sunday morning, the smell of the kitchen, her voice saying "of course it does" — those didn't come from your grief, they came from your *bond* with her, and that bond exists independently of the pain. The grief isn't the thread; *she* is the thread — and she was clearly too deliberate, too present a person to disappear just because you start to heal. What would it mean to you if staying connected to her could actually look like carrying her forward into your life, rather than staying behind with the loss?

client: That distinction — the grief isn't the thread, she is — actually landed somewhere different for me, and I felt something shift just slightly when you said it. But I'm also a little afraid to hold onto that idea too tightly, because what does "carrying her forward" actually look like in practice on a random Tuesday when everything just feels gray and I'm eating lunch alone? I can grasp the concept right now in this room, but I worry it'll evaporate the moment I'm back in my regular life.
therapist: That shift you felt is real and worth trusting, even if it feels fragile right now — and your worry about it evaporating is actually a really practical, grounded instinct rather than a setback. "Carrying her forward" on a gray Tuesday might look less like a feeling and more like a small, concrete action — maybe it's making those thick pancakes once, or pausing at lunch to think "she would have had something funny to say about this," tiny moments where you deliberately invoke her presence rather than waiting for it to arrive. What's one small thing, something she would have recognized as *you*, that you could imagine doing this week that might feel like a quiet nod to her?

client: She used to love that I'd call her just to read her something interesting I'd come across — an article, a weird fact, something that made me think of her. So maybe I could do something like that, write down something I would have called her about, just to keep that habit alive in some form. But I'll be honest, even imagining it makes my throat tighten, because it would just remind me there's no one on the other end of that call anymore.
therapist: That idea is so genuinely beautiful, and it says everything about who she raised you to be — someone who notices the world and wants to share it. The throat tightening makes complete sense, because you're not just imagining a ritual, you're feeling the absence at the other end of it, and that's real and it's going to hurt at first. But I wonder if the ache you'd feel writing that first entry might also be, in its own quiet way, exactly the kind of connection you're afraid of losing — her still being the person you want to tell things to. Would you be willing to try it just once this week, not to feel better necessarily, but just to see what's actually there when you do?

client: I think I can try it once — just once feels manageable in a way that "start a new habit" wouldn't, so framing it that way actually helps. I'm still a little worried I'll sit down to do it and just fall apart completely, and then I'll feel worse instead of better and maybe convince myself the whole thing was a bad idea. But I guess you did say not to expect to feel better, just to see what's there, and maybe that's a low enough bar that I won't talk myself out of it before Tuesday.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in the fact that you just talked yourself through your own doubt in real time — you anticipated the escape hatch and then gently closed it yourself, which is exactly the kind of thing she'd probably have called "not being ridiculous." And if you do sit down and fall apart, that's not the exercise failing — that's the exercise working, because it means you showed up and she was there. What would you want to say to yourself afterward, whatever happens, just for having tried?

client: I think I'd want to say something like "you did something hard and she would have been proud of you" — but even forming that sentence right now makes my eyes sting a little. It's strange because that feels like a kinder thing to say to myself than I'd normally manage, I'm usually pretty quick to just move on or criticize myself for falling apart. Maybe that's part of what I need to practice too, not just the writing, but whatever comes after it.
therapist: The fact that those words made your eyes sting tells me they hit something true — and I want to gently point out that you just did something you said you rarely do: you offered yourself real kindness, unprompted, in the same breath as acknowledging something hard. That *is* the practice, not just the writing but the moment afterward where you choose to meet yourself the way she would have — with warmth instead of a quick move-on. It sounds like she modeled something for you that you're only just beginning to give yourself permission to inherit. What do you think it would look like to treat yourself, even just a little, like someone she loved?
